cover.question: Did daylight saving time start for farmers?

slides.head: The usual story
slides.body: Farmers wanted more daylight in the fields, the story goes, so the government moved the clocks forward for them. The people credited with asking for daylight saving are the people who got rid of it.

slides.head: A wartime fuel measure
slides.body: Germany adopted daylight saving on April 30, 1916 to conserve electricity. The United States copied it in a law enacted March 19, 1918.

slides.head: The 1919 repeal
slides.body: The agriculture industry opposed it from the first season. In 1919 Congress voted to repeal it, President Woodrow Wilson vetoed the repeal twice, and Congress overrode the second veto.

slides.head: Dew, cows and hired hands
slides.body: Farmers waited an extra hour for the dew to evaporate before cutting hay. Hired hands still left at the same time for dinner. Cows were not ready to be milked an hour earlier.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: No. American farmers did not lobby for daylight saving. Agrarian interests led the fight that repealed national daylight saving in 1919.

caption:
Farmers get the blame for daylight saving time. In 1919 they were the ones who got it repealed.

Vetoing the repeal for a second time on August 15, Wilson still conceded "the very considerable and in some respects very serious inconveniences to which the daylight-saving law subjects the farmers of the country". There was then no federal daylight saving observance from 1920 through 1941. Benjamin Franklin gets credit too, but his 1784 letter never proposes moving a clock: it proposes church bells and cannon fire to wake Paris.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Who were you told daylight saving time was for?

cover.question: Why were the catacombs built?

slides.head: Two cities, two reasons
slides.body: Rome's catacombs were dug as cemeteries. Paris's were stone quarries first and an ossuary later. The two have almost nothing in common.

slides.head: Rome: the law kept the dead out
slides.body: Rome's Twelve Tables ruled: "A dead person shall not be buried or burned in the city." So Christians dug outside the walls, into soft volcanic tuff, storey after storey of graves.

slides.head: No evidence of hiding
slides.body: In 257 the prefect of Egypt barred Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria from entering "the so called cemeteries". The Roman state knew where Christian cemeteries were.

slides.head: Paris: the road that fell in
slides.body: In 1774, three hundred metres of a Paris road dropped into old quarry tunnels. On 7 April 1786 a disused quarry was consecrated as the city's ossuary, and bones were carted in at night.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Rome dug its catacombs as community cemeteries outside the city walls. Paris turned worked-out limestone quarries into an ossuary for bones from its former cemeteries.

caption:
Rome and Paris both have catacombs. Only one of the two cities ever set out to dig a cemetery.

Rome's San Callisto catacombs run "about 12 miles long, in four levels, more than twenty meters deep", and their custodians count roughly half a million Christian burials there, including 16 popes. Paris took the name "Catacombs" from Rome when it consecrated its ossuary. The word itself first belonged to one site, the complex of St Sebastian on the Appian Way.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Were you taught that early Christians hid in the catacombs?

cover.question: How do planes fly?
cover.teaser: The air on top arrives first.

slides.head: The school drawing
slides.body: Air splits at the front of a wing. The top path is longer, so that air must go faster to meet the air below at the back edge, and faster air has lower pressure. That is the classroom story.

slides.head: The smoke film
slides.body: In Holger Babinsky's Cambridge wind-tunnel film, the air over the top "has already gone past the end of the wing" while the air underneath is still moving along the lower surface.

slides.head: Where equal transit fails
slides.body: NASA calls equal transit "the most popular incorrect theory of lift", one that predicts "much less than the observed lift". It also cannot explain upside-down flight at all.

slides.head: Flat wings fly too
slides.body: A sail is the same length on both sides and still lifts, because it is curved when rigged. Paper planes with flat sheet wings fly. What a flat wing needs is an angle into the oncoming air.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Wings are shaped and tilted to turn the oncoming air downward, and the air pushes the wings up in return. That turned flow also leaves lower pressure above the wing than below it.

caption:
The classroom story says air over a wing races to meet the air below it. Nothing makes the two meet.

Babinsky said that when he asked school audiences who had heard the story, "every time 95% of the audience puts their hand up." The air over the top really is faster and the pressure there lower; part of the trouble is the route to that answer. Scientific American reports "little, if any, serious disagreement" over the equations aircraft designers solve. What experts still argue over is how to explain lift in a single sentence.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

How were you taught that wings work?

cover.question: What came first, the chicken or the egg?

slides.head: The 2010 headline
slides.body: In July 2010 the story went round that British scientists had settled it in the chicken's favour. The paper behind it was about an eggshell protein called ovocleidin-17.

slides.head: A chemistry simulation
slides.body: The study was a computer simulation of calcium carbonate crystallising into calcite. It dated nothing and examined no fossils.

slides.head: The first amniotes
slides.body: Clawed footprints on a slab from Victoria, Australia, were left by a true amniote, the group that today includes reptiles, birds and mammals. The rock is probably 358.9 to 354 million years old.

slides.head: The first chickens
slides.body: The first unambiguous domestic chicken bones come from Ban Non Wat in Thailand, dated to about 1650 to 1250 BCE.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: The egg came first, by hundreds of millions of years. Eggs existed long before any chicken did.

caption:
The study said to prove the chicken came first never dated anything or looked at a fossil.

The hard chalky shell the riddle pictures turns up much later in the fossil record: the oldest known amniote eggs are 195 to 192 million years old. A 2022 PNAS team assessed more than 600 sites in 89 countries and found older claims of chickens in the Yellow River basin unsupported. There is no single first chicken either, because domestication is a process.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Which answer to this riddle did you grow up with?

cover.question: Why is the keyboard QWERTY and not ABC?

slides.head: The popular story
slides.body: QWERTY was deliberately designed to slow typists down, the story goes, because they typed faster than the machine could handle. There is no evidence for it.

slides.head: A piano-style start
slides.body: In 1868 Sholes, Glidden and Soule patented a typewriter with a keyboard "similar to the keyboard of a piano." A telegraph school advertised it as producing letters "faster than the most rapid penman".

slides.head: Built for Morse
slides.body: Kyoto researchers Koichi and Motoko Yasuoka call the slow-down claim nonsense, because the early keyboard was developed for telegraph operators copying Morse, who had to keep pace with the sender.

slides.head: Reshuffled through 1882
slides.body: Remington's mechanics reworked it and Sholes had Y moved beside T. In 1882 the sales firm Wyckoff, Seamans & Benedict moved M next to N and swapped C and X to evade older patents.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: The keyboard started out alphabetical and was rearranged a few letters at a time between 1868 and 1882. By the 1890s, changing it cost more than keeping it.

caption:
QWERTY was never designed to slow typists down. An 1868 ad sold the typewriter as faster than a pen.

Every letter of TYPEWRITER sits on the top row, but the story that this was arranged for salesmen stays unproven. The big claims for the rival Dvorak layout trace to a 1944 Navy study that, by Earle Strong's account, was conducted by Dvorak himself. A simulation by Donald Norman and David Rumelhart put Dvorak only about 5% faster for expert typists.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What were you told about why the letters are in this order?

cover.question: Why do flies rub their hands?

slides.head: The scheming look
slides.body: A fly rubbing its front legs together looks like a stage villain rubbing his palms, so people read plotting into it. Nothing in the fly supports that.

slides.head: Taste in the feet
slides.body: A fruit fly has approximately 250 taste bristles on its mouthparts and legs. A fly that walks across your plate has already sampled it before its mouthparts arrive.

slides.head: Grip in the feet too
slides.body: The same feet carry adhesive pads covered in hairs. Dirt costs grip: in a 2017 study of dock beetles, which climb on similar pads, soiled pads slipped 10 times further than clean ones.

slides.head: Head first
slides.body: Dusty fruit flies clean in a priority order: eyes, antennae, abdomen, wings, thorax. Between sweeps they rub their legs together, likely scraping off the dust they just collected.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Flies rub their legs together to clean them. Those legs carry much of a fly's sense of taste and all of its grip.

caption:
The fly on your glass is not plotting. It is cleaning the feet it tastes with.

Bitter-taste neurons in a fly's legs also respond to molecules that coat the outside of many bacteria, and that response triggers grooming. Decapitated fruit flies still groomed when bacterial lipopolysaccharide was touched to their legs. All that grooming does not leave a fly germ-free: washing flies caught in cities yielded up to 30,000 bacterial colonies per fly.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What were you told a fly is doing when it rubs its hands?

cover.question: Why do cats like boxes?
cover.teaser: Some sit in squares nobody drew.

slides.head: The usual answers
slides.body: Warmth and a snug fit are two of the usual answers. The best-tested reason is a third one: a box is a place to hide.

slides.head: Shelter trials
slides.body: At a Dutch shelter, 12 of 23 newly arrived cats got a cardboard hiding box. They reached a steady stress level seven days earlier than the rest.

slides.head: A square of tape
slides.body: In 2017, cat owners on Twitter taped shape outlines to their floors and posted their cats sitting inside them, drawing more than 82,000 retweets.

slides.head: A square that was not there
slides.body: In a 2021 study, owners taped four Pac-Man shapes to floors, cut-out corners facing inward, to make an illusory square. Four cats sat in it seven times. A real square outline drew cats eight times.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Cats use boxes to hide, and in shelters a hiding box lowers stress. Why some sit in taped squares is not known. Only 9 of the 30 cats that finished the 2021 study ever chose a shape.

caption:
Four pet cats sat inside a square made of nothing but four Pac-Man shapes taped to the floor.

In head-to-head pairings, the illusion beat a control made of the same shapes turned outward 5 to 0. The authors concluded that cats "may treat the subjective Kanizsa contours as they do real contours." Owners were asked to wear dark sunglasses so they could not cue their cats. In the 2019 shelter trial, the box made no significant difference to weight loss or adoption rates.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Has your cat ever sat in a shape taped or drawn on the floor?

cover.question: Where do hamsters come from?

slides.head: April 12, 1930
slides.body: A hunter named Tah'an and a crew of villagers dug a mother and her litter out of a wheat field near Aleppo, Syria. Israel Aharoni, a biologist from Jerusalem, had come to catch one.

slides.head: One brother, one sister
slides.body: Three littermates, one male and two females, were kept to start a breeding colony in Jerusalem. A single brother-sister pair from them founded the line.

slides.head: From one litter
slides.body: Nearly every laboratory golden hamster descends from that one litter, and Rob Dunn, writing in Smithsonian magazine, says every domestic one does. Descendants reached the United States in 1938.

slides.head: Wild and Endangered
slides.body: Wild golden hamsters are listed as Endangered. On the Syrian-Turkish border they are treated as crop pests, trapped or poisoned in February.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Hamsters come from Europe and Asia. The usual pet, the golden or Syrian hamster, is native to farm fields around Aleppo in northern Syria and southern Turkey.

caption:
Nearly every pet golden hamster traces back to one litter dug out of a Syrian wheat field in 1930.

The dig was for Saul Adler, who wanted a laboratory animal that could be infected with Leishmania parasites. The species was not new to science: George Robert Waterhouse had shown it to the Zoological Society of London as a new species in 1839. Dwarf hamsters belong to a different genus, and come from the dry steppe and desert of central Asia.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Where were you told pet hamsters come from?

cover.question: What does AM stand for?
cover.teaser: Noon is neither AM nor PM.

slides.head: The everyday rule
slides.body: By everyday convention, 12 a.m. is midnight and 12 p.m. is noon. Britain's National Physical Laboratory says no official standard fixes either meaning.

slides.head: The Latin
slides.body: AM stands for ante meridiem, Latin for "before noon," and PM for post meridiem, "after noon." At noon itself the time is not before noon and not after it.

slides.head: The style manual flip
slides.body: The US government's own style manual called noon 12 a.m. and midnight 12 p.m. in its 2000 edition. Its 2008 edition reversed both. In 1984 it had written noon as 12 m.

slides.head: What timekeepers advise
slides.body: NIST says "12 a.m. and 12 p.m. are ambiguous and should not be used." Britain's NPL says it is always best to use the words midday, noon and midnight.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: AM means before noon and PM means after noon, so noon is strictly neither. Calling it 12 p.m. is only a convention.

caption:
AM means before noon and PM means after noon. Noon itself fits neither label.

The word noon once meant 3 p.m.: Old English non, the ninth hour from sunrise. The shift toward midday began in the 12th century. Latin meridies, behind both abbreviations, meant both noon and south. For contracts and insurance policies, NIST suggests writing 11:59 p.m. or 12:01 a.m., since midnight on a given date can mean either end of the day.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

How were you taught to write noon and midnight?

cover.question: Why are veins blue?

slides.head: Wrong answer one: blue blood
slides.body: Diagrams print veins blue. But human blood is red at every oxygen level: bright red when it carries oxygen, dark red when it has lost it.

slides.head: Wrong answer two: blue light
slides.body: The usual correction says skin scatters a lot of the red light, leaving blue light to reflect off the blood and back to your eyes. Measurement points the other way.

slides.head: The 2026 phantom study
slides.body: Researchers photographed artificial vessels buried in synthetic skin. Above the vein, "in absolute terms, more red light is reflected than blue light".

slides.head: It is contrast
slides.body: Red light reaches the vein and is absorbed there, so the skin over it returns less red than the skin beside it. Human colour vision reads that local shortfall of red as blue.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Veins look blue because of contrast, not because anything inside them is blue. The blood was dark red the whole time.

caption:
Veins look blue, yet in a 2026 optics study more red light than blue came back from above an artificial vein.

Depth decided what showed: at 1.5 and 2.0 mm below the synthetic skin's surface, the blue was nearly indistinguishable whatever the oxygen level. The phantoms matched only one pale skin type, and the authors ask future work to explore the role of melanin. Blue blood does exist in horseshoe crabs: copper-based and straw-coloured, turning blue when it meets high concentrations of oxygen.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Were you taught that the blood in your veins is blue?

cover.question: Why do we celebrate Veterans Day?

slides.head: The eleventh hour
slides.body: Veterans Day began as Armistice Day, for the 11 a.m. ceasefire of 1918. That deadline was the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month.

slides.head: One word crossed out
slides.body: In 1954 Congress amended the 1938 act "by striking out the word 'Armistice' and inserting in its place the word 'Veterans.'" November 11 then honored American veterans of all wars.

slides.head: The October years
slides.body: The Uniform Holiday Bill, signed on June 28, 1968, moved it to the fourth Monday in October. The first under that law "was observed with much confusion on October 25, 1971."

slides.head: Back to November 11
slides.body: By 1975, 46 states had either never changed the date or returned to November 11. A 1975 law returned the federal holiday to November 11 beginning in 1978.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Veterans Day thanks everyone who served honorably in the US military, in wartime or peacetime. The VA says it is largely intended to thank living veterans.

caption:
For seven years, the federal Veterans Day fell in October, not on November 11.

Private Henry Gunther's death was recorded at 10:59 a.m. on November 11, 1918, one minute before the armistice took effect. Since 2016, federal law has directed the president to issue a proclamation each year calling for two minutes of silence on the day, beginning at 2:11 p.m. eastern standard time. The VA spells it Veterans Day, with no apostrophe.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Were you taught why it falls on November 11?

cover.question: What was Einstein's IQ?
cover.teaser: The 160 has no test behind it.

slides.head: The famous number
slides.body: The figure usually quoted is 160. In 2022 The Independent, setting a schoolboy beside Stephen Hawking, wrote that Einstein "is said to have had an IQ of around 160, although it is unclear whether either man did a test."

slides.head: No test on record
slides.body: There is no record that Einstein ever took an intelligence test. The Army Alpha of 1917, which psychologist Russell Warne calls the first successful one for adults, came when Einstein was 38.

slides.head: From 150 to 207
slides.body: LIFE's arithmetic gave 205 in 1945, and in 1954 it printed an estimate of 192. Popular Mechanics gave an estimated 207 in 1962 while calling him a man "who never took an intelligence test." Outliers said 150 in 2008.

slides.head: A father's question
slides.body: In 1954 a father recalled being told his son's IQ was 185, asking, "Genius is about 160, isn't it?" and hearing, "Albert Einstein's is probably a little higher." Whether that meant above 160 or 185 is unclear.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Nobody knows Einstein's IQ. In 2023 Warne concluded that "any currently existing claims of an IQ score for Albert Einstein are not credible."

caption:
Einstein's IQ has been given as 150, 160, 192, 205 and 207, and no test lies behind any of them.

When Russell Warne searched for a score in 2023, he found no figure from Einstein's lifetime older than LIFE's 1945 story. The story that Einstein failed math is wrong too: his 1896 school-leaving certificate gave him the top grade of 6 in algebra, geometry and physics. Shown a clipping in 1935 that said he had failed, he replied, "I never failed in mathematics".

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What number were you told for Einstein's IQ?

cover.question: Why is the Illuminati on the dollar bill?

slides.head: The story
slides.body: A shadowy society called the Illuminati has secretly run world affairs for centuries, the story goes, and signs its work with the eye and pyramid on the one-dollar bill.

slides.head: The real Illuminati
slides.body: Adam Weishaupt founded the Illuminati of Bavaria on May 1, 1776. It took the owl of Minerva as its symbol. Edicts to suppress it followed in 1784 and 1785.

slides.head: The Great Seal, 1782
slides.body: The eye and pyramid are the reverse of the Great Seal of the United States, adopted by Congress on June 20, 1782. Charles Thomson explained: "The pyramid signifies strength and duration."

slides.head: Thirteen steps
slides.body: The official 1782 description sets no number of steps. The thirteen steps on the dollar are a tradition. Both sides of the seal reached the one-dollar note in 1935.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: The Illuminati is not on the dollar. The eye and pyramid come from the Great Seal, and Thomson said the eye alludes to interventions of providence "in favor of the American cause."

caption:
The real Illuminati took the owl of Minerva as its symbol and was outlawed in Bavaria by 1785.

The eye was in the very first design for the seal, and Congress received that design on August 20, 1776. Novus Ordo Seclorum means a new order of the ages, not New World Order. Henry Wallace later said he gave Franklin Roosevelt the idea of putting the seal's reverse on the money, a claim the official history says cannot be verified in official records.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What were you told the eye on the dollar meant?

cover.question: Why do hyenas laugh?
cover.teaser: It is the sound of losing.

slides.head: The pop-culture version
slides.body: The pop-culture hyena cackles because it is amused, mocking something weaker than itself. The recordings point the other way.

slides.head: Kept off the kill
slides.body: Spotted hyenas giggle mostly during food fights. Observers in the wild had long heard it from animals kept off a kill by higher-ranking clanmates.

slides.head: 1,807 notes
slides.body: A 2010 study of 17 captive spotted hyenas recorded 254 giggle bouts containing 1,807 notes. Mean pitch ran from about 650 Hz at two years old to under 450 Hz by twenty.

slides.head: Rank in the wobble
slides.body: Timbre varied more in subordinate animals than in dominant ones. The researchers suggest a dominant hyena might let a subordinate eat to stop it giggling and drawing competitors.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: A hyena's giggle is not amusement. Researchers read it as a sign of submission and frustration, and it can carry clues to the caller's age, identity and rank.

caption:
The giggling hyena at a carcass is often the one being kept from the food.

The famous giggle belongs to the spotted hyena, and the brown hyena lacks it altogether. The hyena's other famous call, the whoop, can be heard up to 5 km away. Despite the doglike look, hyenas sit in Feliformia, the cat side of the order Carnivora.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Have you ever heard hyenas giggle, in the wild or at a zoo?

cover.question: Why is it called an em dash?
cover.teaser: An em is not a letter.

slides.head: A square of metal
slides.body: In 1919 A.A. Stewart's primer for printing apprentices explained that an em "is a square of the body," which "varies in size with each size of type."

slides.head: 12 points wide
slides.body: Stewart's arithmetic: "a 12-point em is 12 points deep and 12 points wide." The em dash was cast one em wide, so its width changed with the type.

slides.head: The M does not fill it
slides.body: The unit took its name from the capital M. Yet in ordinary roman fonts, the bibliographer Ronald McKerrow wrote, the M is narrower than its height.

slides.head: Mutton and nut
slides.body: The en is half an em. To tell the two apart out loud, printers called them mutton and nut, and the dashes the mutton dash and the nut dash.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: It is called an em dash because it was cast one em wide, and an em is a unit equal to the type size. A capital M set in 12-point type is not 12 points of anything.

caption:
An em dash in a headline is physically longer than an em dash in the footnote below it.

On the typewriter the dash became two hyphens struck in a row, and a 1902 manual told typists, "Strike the hyphen twice to make the dash." Matthew Butterick writes that today's digital fonts make the dash typically about as wide as a capital H. A March 2026 preprint found em dash rates ranging from none at all in Meta's Llama models to 10.62 per 1,000 words for GPT-4.1.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Were you taught to type two hyphens for a dash?

cover.question: When was the fax machine invented?

slides.head: An office machine
slides.body: Fax machines filled offices in the 1980s. Yet a fax machine was patented nearly 33 years before Bell's telephone patent.

slides.head: A clockmaker's patent
slides.body: Alexander Bain, a Scottish clockmaker, patented a fax machine on 27 May 1843. His patent describes copying printer's type at a distance with two pendulums kept in step by electricity.

slides.head: Printed in dots
slides.body: At the receiving end, current marked chemically soaked damp paper, "which will produce a copy of the printing surface of the types in a series of small dots."

slides.head: Paris to Lyon, 1865
slides.body: Giovanni Caselli's pantelegraph ran the first commercial fax service, between Paris and Lyon, from 1865. In 1866, 4,853 of 4,860 transmissions "involved finance or business."

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: The fax machine was invented in 1843. Paris was faxing Lyon in 1865, 11 years before Bell patented the telephone.

caption:
Paris was sending handwriting to Lyon by wire 11 years before Bell patented the telephone.

Bain's copier was the seventh of nine improvements claimed for clocks and telegraphs in his 1843 patent. On Caselli's machine, by Robert Sabine's arithmetic, a sheet holding about twenty-five written words took 1 minute 48 seconds. Xerox's Magnafax Telecopier, delivered in July 1966, could send a letter-size page over an ordinary phone line in six minutes.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

When did you last send or receive a fax?

cover.question: Why do we only see one side of the Moon?

slides.head: Two mistakes
slides.body: The hidden hemisphere is still routinely called the dark side. A second mistake travels with the nickname: the idea that the Moon does not spin at all.

slides.head: Spin and orbit match
slides.body: The Moon rotates once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth, roughly 27.3 days. Astronomers call this tidal locking.

slides.head: A Moon that stopped
slides.body: A Moon that had stopped rotating would show Earth every side of itself once a month. The unchanging face is what a rotating Moon looks like from the body it is locked to.

slides.head: Not dark, just far
slides.body: The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side. Dark meant unknown, not unlit. Luna 3 first photographed it on 7 October 1959.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: We see one side because the Moon spins once per orbit, so the same hemisphere stays pointed at Earth. A wobble called libration shows us about 59% of the surface over time.

caption:
The Moon does spin. It turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to go once around Earth.

Earth's gravity raised a bulge in the young Moon, and the tug of war slowed its spin until a single spin took the same time as one trip around Earth. The same process is slowing Earth: one study puts the tidal lengthening of the day at 2.395 milliseconds per century. Dark maria cover about 30 percent of the near side but only about 2 percent of the far side.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Were you taught that the far side is the dark side?

cover.question: How is gold formed?
cover.teaser: Stars made it, then Earth swallowed it.

slides.head: Not in the ground
slides.body: Gold is formed in space, not in the ground. Fusion in stars stops at iron, because "iron releases no energy when fused."

slides.head: A flood of neutrons
slides.body: Iron has 26 protons and gold has 79. Gold forms mostly when rare cataclysms like neutron-star collisions flood nuclei with neutrons faster than they can decay.

slides.head: The 2017 collision
slides.body: In 2017 astronomers caught two neutron stars colliding in a galaxy about 130 million light years away. From the glow, researchers estimated a yield of around 200 Earth masses of gold.

slides.head: Into the core
slides.body: As Earth formed, molten iron sank to make the core. More than 99% of Earth's gold lies there, under about 3,000 km of solid rock.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Gold is made in space, mostly in rare blasts like neutron-star collisions. The gold we mine is thought to have come later on meteorites, gathered into quartz veins and river gravels.

caption:
Every gold ring, coin and circuit board ever made came out of the sliver of gold outside Earth's core.

Greenland rocks some 3.8 billion years old carry a tungsten difference "in good agreement" with a late meteorite shower. In 2025 a Goettingen team reported material from the core, including gold, leaking into the mantle. Astronomers still cannot account for all the gold in the galaxy.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

Have you ever panned for gold, or seen it in a river?

cover.question: Why is it called a poop deck?
cover.teaser: Crew toilets were at the bow.

slides.head: The joke
slides.body: One belief says the deck is named after what sailors did there. That pun needs a meaning the word did not carry when the stern got its name.

slides.head: Poop meant stern
slides.body: Poop is an old word for a ship's stern, going back to the Latin puppis. The OED's earliest example of that sense, from 1489, reads: "The pouppe whiche is the hindermost partye of the shippe."

slides.head: The other poop
slides.body: The sense of breaking wind is first recorded in 1689. Poop meaning excrement dates to 1744 at the earliest, and Merriam-Webster dates the compound poop deck to 1717.

slides.head: Toilets at the bow
slides.body: The crew's toilets, called the head, were at the bow. On USS Constitution they were four or six holes cut in a plank overhanging the water.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: The poop deck is named for the poop, an old word for a ship's stern, recorded in English by 1489, two centuries before poop had any bodily sense.

caption:
Poop meant a ship's stern two centuries before it had any bodily sense in English.

The myth still lands near something real: the captain's private privy was in a quarter gallery at the stern. In 2005 archaeologists recovered a 31.8-inch lead tube from the stern area of a wreck believed to be Blackbeard's Queen Anne's Revenge, and the project's report identifies it as a seat of ease. Pooped, meaning tired, has no proven link to ships.

What were you told the poop deck was named after?

cover.question: When was Bluetooth invented?

slides.head: Lady Bluetooth
slides.body: A popular story credits Hedy Lamarr with the radio trick behind Bluetooth. Her 1942 patent did use frequency hopping, but a 1908 book had already described it.

slides.head: Lund, 1994
slides.body: Bluetooth was invented at Ericsson in Lund, Sweden, where the main design work began in 1994. Jaap Haartsen and Sven Mattisson turned the idea into a working radio.

slides.head: A Viking king
slides.body: The codename honored Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century king of Denmark. The standard was meant to unite computers and phones the way he united the Danes.

slides.head: PAN won 4-1
slides.body: The official name "went to PAN in a 4-1 vote." PAN could not be trademarked, and the backup, RadioWire, had not been searched in time.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Bluetooth was invented at Ericsson, with main design work from 1994 and the 1.0 specification in 1999. Its name was only a stand-in codename that stuck.

caption:
Bluetooth's name was only ever meant as a placeholder until marketing found something better.

Intel engineer Jim Kardach came up with the codename after, by his own account, Ericsson's Sven Mattisson retold Scandinavian history on a Toronto pub crawl. Ericsson's marketers had floated Flirt, "Getting close without touching." The logo is a bind rune of Harald's initials, H and B.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What was the first gadget you paired over Bluetooth?

cover.question: How are TVs measured?
cover.teaser: Diagonally, but US law said width.

slides.head: The number on the box
slides.body: TVs are measured diagonally, from one corner of the visible picture to the opposite corner. The bezel, frame and stand are not counted.

slides.head: The 1966 rule
slides.body: A Federal Trade Commission rule took effect on July 1, 1966. Unless the seller said otherwise, a TV's size meant the width of its picture.

slides.head: Sized like a rug
slides.body: Blankets were sized as "76 x 107 inches" and rugs as "9 ft. x 12 ft.," so the FTC concluded shoppers would take a "19 inch set" to mean a picture 19 inches across.

slides.head: The repeal
slides.body: Manufacturers kept the diagonal. Repealing the rule in 2018, effective January 7, 2019, the FTC found that "the industry universally measures television screen sizes using the diagonal dimension."

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: TVs are sold by the diagonal of the visible picture. But for 52 and a half years, a US rule made width the default, and the diagonal needed a label.

caption:
For 52 and a half years, a US rule said a TV's size, unless the seller said otherwise, meant the width of its picture.

Many sizes on the box are rounded class figures: in ENERGY STAR's list of certified TVs, most sets near 65 inches measure 64.5 inches corner to corner. At the same diagonal, a 16:9 screen is wider but shorter than a 4:3 one and has about 11 percent less area. In 2018 the Consumer Technology Association noted that the FTC had not brought an enforcement action under the rule "in the more than 50 years since its adoption."

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

cover.question: Why do whales explode?

slides.head: Florence, Oregon, 1970
slides.body: On 12 November 1970, a 45-foot sperm whale had been rotting on the beach for three days. The state Highway Division found no rendering plant that wanted it.

slides.head: Half a ton of dynamite
slides.body: A highway crew placed twenty 50-pound cases of explosives under the whale. The blast raised a 100-foot high column of sand and whale.

slides.head: Over the crowd
slides.body: A three-foot chunk sailed over the crowd and crushed the roof of Walter Umenhofer's 1969 Oldsmobile. Assistant district engineer George Thornton's verdict: "It went just exactly right."

slides.head: What nature does
slides.body: Gut bacteria do fill a dead whale's sealed carcass with gas, mostly carbon dioxide. But most documented bursts were set off by people blowing up, cutting into or trucking the whale.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: A dead whale bloats as its own bacteria keep working, and pressure rises. What turns one into footage is nearly always a person with a knife, a truck or dynamite.

caption:
Oregon's famous exploding whale did not burst on its own. The state blew it up with half a ton of dynamite in 1970.

Thornton had ruled out burial because "these things have a tendency to just get uncovered again." Umenhofer, who had demolitions experience from the service, felt the shot was improperly placed and overloaded, and the Highway Division's insurer paid him the car's full retail value. Today NOAA Fisheries lists burial, towing offshore, rendering and other options for a dead whale. Explosives are not among them.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

cover.question: What is the biggest number?

slides.head: The infinity answer
slides.body: Ask for the biggest number and some people say infinity. But infinity is not a number you can reach by counting, so it does not win.

slides.head: The googol
slides.body: Edward Kasner's nine-year-old nephew named 1 followed by 100 zeros the googol. At the same time he named a bigger number, the googolplex, which became 1 followed by a googol of zeros.

slides.head: Graham's number
slides.body: In 1977 Martin Gardner reported it held "the record for the largest number ever used in a serious mathematical proof." No one can write it out in ordinary digits, yet its final digits end in 4195387.

slides.head: Bigger still
slides.body: Harvey Friedman's TREE(3), from a game with trees, makes Graham's number look "puny." Agustin Rayo won a 2007 MIT duel with a number described by a formula of second-order set theory.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: There is no biggest number. Add 1 to any number, however huge, and you get a bigger one. Like every number before it, Rayo's number loses to itself plus 1.

caption:
There is no biggest number. In 2007, two philosophers held a duel at MIT to write one anyway.

Only finite numbers counted, and it was unsporting to win by adding one to the other side's last entry. The two men wanted, in Rayo's words, "a war of originality, not a war of patience". Google took its name from the googol: "we liked the spelling 'Google' better," its 1999 website said.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

cover.question: When did the Mayflower land?

slides.head: Cape Cod first
slides.body: The Mayflower anchored off what is now Provincetown on 11 November 1620, and a party went ashore that day. The ship could get no closer than three quarters of a mile, so people had to "wade a bow shot or two."

slides.head: Plymouth a month later
slides.body: A small boat party went ashore at Plymouth on 11 December 1620. The ship followed and anchored there on 16 December.

slides.head: Two calendars
slides.body: Those are the Old Style dates the passengers wrote. In 1620 England's calendar ran 10 days behind today's, so the landings fall on 21 November and 21 December.

slides.head: No rock in the accounts
slides.body: The two accounts by people who were there mention no rock in describing the landing. Thomas Faunce, a church elder in his nineties, pointed out the rock about 1741, citing his father, who arrived in 1623.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: The Mayflower landed twice: at Cape Cod on 11 November 1620 and at Plymouth a month later. Plymouth Rock as the landing place is an unverified tradition.

caption:
The Mayflower first landed at Cape Cod, not Plymouth. Plymouth came a month later, found by a small boat.

Before going ashore at Cape Cod, the men signed the agreement now called the Mayflower Compact. The Atlantic crossing took 66 days. Within two or three months, Bradford wrote, "halfe of their company dyed." The rock first reached print in 1775.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What were you taught at school about the Pilgrims and Plymouth Rock?

cover.question: What is a group of turkeys called?

slides.head: The trivia answer
slides.body: Trivia lists say a group of turkeys is a rafter, a word with the ring of a medieval hunting term. It has not been traced in print before 1908.

slides.head: No turkeys on medieval lists
slides.body: Many famous group names come from fifteenth-century lists, like the Book of St Albans in 1486. The turkey, native to North America, reached Europe only in the sixteenth century.

slides.head: Flock and gang
slides.body: Flock, for turkeys, was in print by 1657. Gang, the hunters' word, was in print by 1709, in John Lawson's A New Voyage to Carolina: his party passed "great Gangs of Turkies."

slides.head: Rafter, 1908
slides.body: Rafter's trail, as far as digitized books go, begins with Herbert Knight Horsfield's English Bird Life in 1908: "A rafter of Turkeys." He names no fowler and cites no book.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: A group of turkeys is called a flock. Gang is the hunters' word. Rafter is the trivia answer, and it has the shortest paper trail of the three.

caption:
Rafter, the trivia word for a group of turkeys, sounds medieval. It has not been traced in print before 1908.

On large tobacco farms a gang of turkeys had a job: an 1821 article in the Baltimore farm paper American Farmer recommended raising turkeys to eat the worms. The popular story that rafter comes from turkeys roosting in barn rafters is unverified, and wild turkeys roost in trees. Hunters still use the word gang: the National Wild Turkey Federation says young males "usually travel in jake gangs."

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What word for a group of turkeys did you grow up hearing?

cover.question: Why does turkey make you sleepy?

slides.head: The tryptophan myth
slides.body: The story blames turkey's tryptophan. The brain does build serotonin from tryptophan. The weak link is getting more tryptophan into the brain.

slides.head: Per 100 grams
slides.body: Roasted turkey breast: 0.287 or 0.364 grams of tryptophan, depending on the USDA sample. Roasted chicken breast: 0.362 grams. Hard parmesan: 0.482 grams.

slides.head: The 1972 rat study
slides.body: Fernstrom and Wurtman found that diets containing protein pushed blood tryptophan up in rats, yet brain tryptophan and serotonin did not change.

slides.head: Outnumbered
slides.body: Five other amino acids compete with tryptophan "for uptake into the brain." In USDA's roasted turkey breast records, those five outweigh the tryptophan roughly 18 to 1.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: A meal, the mid-afternoon body-clock dip and alcohol can all make people sleepy. Turkey is not special: it has about as much tryptophan as chicken breast.

caption:
Chicken breast has about as much tryptophan as turkey breast, and parmesan has more.

In a 1998 study, 16 men and women were measurably sleepier 1.5 hours after a meal than before it, whether the meal was high in fat or high in carbohydrate. In a 2012 simulator study, young men who had slept five hours drifted out of lane more after a 922-calorie lunch than a 305-calorie one. The myth was a sitcom plot by 1997, in the Seinfeld episode "The Merv Griffin Show".

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What were you told makes everyone sleepy after Thanksgiving dinner?

cover.question: Why is it called a flea market?

slides.head: The New York story
slides.body: One story credits New York's Fly Market, whose name came from Dutch. But the Fly Market closed in 1822, 65 years before the earliest known "flea market" in English print.

slides.head: Copenhagen, 1887
slides.body: The earliest known English example, from 29 May 1887, is a letter about a Copenhagen market of second-hand clothes and rags. "Perhaps the fleas had killed it," it said.

slides.head: A jeer in Brest
slides.body: In October 1890 a Brest paper called the town's yearly fair "le marche aux puces," the flea market. Fourteen of the town's women resellers signed a protest in elegant calligraphy.

slides.head: Flea, not flee
slides.body: Another story says Paris dealers were forced to flee. But the 1887 letter already means the insect, and Merriam-Webster notes "considerably more evidence for flea than flee."

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: A flea market is named for the insect. The name mocked markets of secondhand clothes and rags that people believed carried fleas, and it stuck anyway.

caption:
Flea market began as a jeer: a mocking name for markets of secondhand rags people believed carried fleas.

In July 1891 the Yorkshire Evening Post reported that at the Paris market its regulars called the Flea Market, an old woman had cut open a secondhand mattress and found 14,000 francs in gold. The Saint-Ouen market's own history calls the name anonymous and dates it to about 1904. With about 1,100 dealers and galleries, Saint-Ouen now carries the old jeer in its official name.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What were you told about where the name flea market came from?

cover.question: Why are cats afraid of cucumbers?

slides.head: The viral clip
slides.body: A cat eats with its head in the bowl. Someone slides a cucumber behind it. The cat turns and leaves the ground. The caption says cats carry an inherited fear of snakes.

slides.head: The snake evidence
slides.body: Snake-sensitive neurons were reported in 2013 in two Japanese macaques, in a part of the brain the researchers say has no counterpart in non-primate mammals. A cat is one.

slides.head: Cats hunt snakes
slides.body: Pamela Perry of the Cornell Feline Health Center: "Cats don't have a natural fear of snakes. In fact, a lot of them hunt snakes."

slides.head: In the stomachs
slides.body: In southwest Western Australia, six of 358 feral and stray cats whose stomach contents were analyzed had eaten venomous snakes.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: Cats show a startle response, not a cucumber phobia. The prank puts a novel object behind a cat at its bowl, without warning. The snake theory is unverified.

caption:
The cucumber-snake theory has a problem: Cornell's cat behavior expert says a lot of cats hunt snakes.

Neither Cornell's write-up nor National Geographic's cites a study of cats and cucumbers, so the evidence behind both is footage. National Geographic noted that some cats "couldn't care less about the vegetable intrusion." Cornell advises against the prank: a timid cat may attach the fright to its food dish, to the location or to its owner.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

cover.question: Why do people say Xmas?
cover.teaser: A Greek X, nearly 1,000 years old.

slides.head: The complaint
slides.body: Every December someone says Xmas takes the Christ out of Christmas. The X reads as a blank where a name should be.

slides.head: Not an English X
slides.body: The X is the Greek letter chi, the initial of Christos, the Greek word that became Christ in English. The Greek capital chi and the Roman X look the same.

slides.head: The entry for 1021
slides.body: A copy of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle that appears to date from the middle of the 11th century writes Christmas as Xpes maesse, in its entry for 1021.

slides.head: A family of X words
slides.body: The X worked on every word built on Christ's name: Xpen for christen, Xtian for Christian, Xpher for Christopher. Coleridge wrote Xmas in 1801, Byron in 1811.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: The X in Xmas is the Greek initial of Christ. English scribes used it as shorthand for Christ by the 11th century, long before advertising.

caption:
The X in Xmas is not a blank. It is the Greek letter chi, the first letter of Christos.

Merriam-Webster dates Xmas itself to 1721. The objection is real all the same: Lifeway Research reported in December 2018 that 42 percent of Christians say it is offensive when people say X-mas instead of Christmas. Merriam-Webster gives KRIS-mas as the pronunciation and lists EKS-mas only as an alternative.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What were you told the X in Xmas stood for?

cover.question: What is a cookie on a website?

slides.head: A web with no memory
slides.body: HTTP forgot each visitor between pages, so every click arrived as if from a stranger. For a shop, that meant a cart that emptied itself.

slides.head: July 1994
slides.body: Around July 1994, by his own account, Lou Montulli, then 23, heard that a shopping server needed a cart. Within the next week, he recalled, the general idea of web cookies had formed.

slides.head: No compelling reason
slides.body: A server hands the browser a small payload, and the browser hands it back. Netscape's original spec says "the state object is called a cookie, for no compelling reason."

slides.head: Wile E. Coyote's order
slides.body: The spec's worked example is an order: the server sets CUSTOMER=WILE_E_COYOTE, then PART_NUMBER=ROCKET_LAUNCHER_0001, then SHIPPING=FEDEX.

slides.head: The answer
slides.body: A cookie is a small piece of data a website asks your browser to store and send back to that same site. It is how a site remembers a login, a shopping cart or a setting.

caption:
Netscape invented the web cookie in 1994 to make a shopping cart work. Tracking came later.

Montulli's design sent a site's cookie back only to the server that had set it. What he missed, he later wrote, was how cookies would interact with content embedded in a page: ad companies, DoubleClick in particular, used third-party cookies to track a browser across sites. The name came from magic cookie, programmers' slang Montulli had heard in an operating systems course.

The full entry, with every source linked: strictly.fyi (link in bio)

What did you think cookies were the first time a site asked you to accept them?
